title: Describing people
description: Say what someone is like, and what they do.

explanation.summary: Two things meet in this unit. The irregular verbs are the ones Spanish uses most, so their forms are worth learning early. And the adjectives that describe people change their ending to match the noun.

sections.heading: The verbs you cannot avoid
sections.body: Eight verbs are irregular in the present, and they are the ones you use every day: ser, estar, ir, haber, dar, saber, querer, poder. Their forms are worth learning as whole words rather than as a pattern: estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están.

examples.en: I do not know his name.

sections.heading: The adjective endings
sections.body: An adjective ending in -o changes to -a before a feminine noun: un trabajo difícil, una casa difícil. One ending in -e or a consonant does not change: un hombre grande, una mujer grande. And the adjectives of nationality drop their ending in front of a noun: un español alto, una española alta.

examples.es: Mi padre es un médico joven.
examples.en: My father is a young doctor.

sections.heading: Where the adjective goes
sections.body: The adjective goes after the noun: un trabajo difícil. It can also go before, but then it means something more literary, and it is not used with every adjective. In everyday Spanish, put it after.
